blocks.text: Exodus 12 records the institution of Passover, the pivotal moment when the LORD commands Israel to prepare a lamb for household consumption and mark their doorposts with blood. This narrative stands at the center of the exodus tradition, marking the deliverance from slavery and the formation of Israel as a redeemed people. The chapter frames the turning point from Egypt's oppression to liberation, establishing patterns of divine action and covenant remembrance that will shape Israel's identity.

Exodus 12:12 explicitly frames the plague of the firstborn as an act of judgment executed by the LORD against Egypt's gods. The text makes clear that Israel's deliverance involves direct confrontation with Egyptian religious power, not merely a natural disaster. This religious dimension is central to the passage's own interpretation of events, positioning the exodus as YHWH's victory over the divine claims of Egypt's pantheon.

sections.title: Passover as Covenant Sign and Memorial

blocks.text: The blood on the doorposts functions as a covenant sign, marking identity and belonging to the LORD's redeemed people. Passover originates in this exodus deliverance and becomes Israel's annual memorial, renewing the pattern of God hearing suffering and calling his people into freedom. The meal and ritual mark covenant obligation and identity, establishing a practice that binds each generation to the story of redemption.

Egypt functions in the passage as both the place of Israel's suffering and the stage for God's redemptive power. In Israel's theological memory, Egypt represents the bondage from which the LORD delivered his people through direct action. This memory shapes Israel's identity as a redeemed covenant people, whose calendar, worship, and identity are grounded not in human security or imperial stability, but in God's deliverance and presence.
